Feature: pass^k reliability readout + adaptive run-count recommendation
Pain point: A single pass hides whether the agent behaves the same way twice; users ship agents that passed once and fail unpredictably
Label: Proposed
Differentiator angle: Re-running is near-free (deterministic free minting) so k-repeat reliability is economically viable in a way paid/stateful competitor setups are not
Notes: Adaptive form (recommend k from measured variance) beats a static per-task-type rule; pending product check on today's Runs/Insights | 2026-09-29: further supported by 'Same Winners, Different Success Rates' (ordinal measures provably hide reliability); thesis T-01 now near-established
In plain terms: Show, beside a run's score, how often the agent succeeds every single time (not just once), and suggest running a task a few more times when results are inconsistent or just once when they are stable. Helps you trust a result instead of being fooled by one lucky pass.

Feature: Attribution as a location on the trace + every attribution a routed next action
Pain point: Users cannot tell if a failure is the agent's or the environment's; scores are gameable when isolation is weak
Source dates: BenchJack May 2026 read 2026-09-25; HackDetect 2026-07-24 read 2026-09-29; ReplayLens 2026-09-28 + failure-taxonomy 2026-08-26 read 2026-09-29
Label: Proposed
Differentiator angle: Env-vs-agent attribution is THE moat asset; two independent audits prove the failure mode is real and common
Notes: Aligns with v3 direction (failures light up in place) but v1-implementable at the scorecard level | 2026-09-29: reinforced by ReplayLens (agents exploit outcome info) and a 7-category failure taxonomy; thesis T-03 upgraded to strengthening
In plain terms: When an agent fails, point on the trace to exactly where and why it broke and whether it was the agent's fault or the environment's, with a button to jump straight to fixing it. Turns a confusing failure into a clear next step.

Feature: Always show a tradeoff axis (cost or reliability) beside the primary score in comparisons
Pain point: A 1-point accuracy edge can hide a 10x cost difference; single-number rankings mislead
Label: Quick win
Differentiator angle: Extends the shipped refuses-to-average-mismatched-versions guarantee from validity to tradeoff-honesty
Notes: Mostly surfacing data the platform already has (cost measured from real usage); HAL is the reference design
In plain terms: Whenever two runs or models are compared, always show cost (and reliability) right next to the accuracy score, so a tiny accuracy win that actually costs far more is obvious. Stops people picking a winner that is actually a bad deal.

Feature: Feasibility explanation at task authoring (why is this task not solvable)
Pain point: Authors cannot tell whether a task is solvable or why not; agents waste budget barreling ahead on infeasible tasks
Label: Needs evidence
Differentiator angle: LayerLens knows the tools and the answer key so it can compute missing-dependency infeasibility (FeasiGen's masking in reverse)
Notes: Single source; needs a second source or an author-confirmed outcome to reach L1
In plain terms: When someone builds a test task, tell them whether it is actually solvable and, if not, why (for example a tool or record it needs is missing). Saves them from testing agents on impossible tasks.

Feature: Flag same-family judge/agent pairings with a cross-family or Grader suggestion
Pain point: AI judges quietly favor their own model family; verdicts are biased with no visible signal
Source dates: self-preference repo undated read 2026-09-25; identity-conformity 2026-09-27 read 2026-09-29
Label: Proposed
Notes: Upgraded L0->L1 2026-09-29: self-preference now corroborated by an independent 12-model study (C-0014), promoted thesis T-05. Priority jumped 0.90->1.80 (current top item). Cheap to build (metadata comparison + a badge). Next: product check whether Judge vs agent model identity is surfaced today
In plain terms: If the AI grading a result is from the same model family as the agent being graded, show a warning, because judges tend to favor their own family. Keeps a hidden bias from quietly skewing verdicts.

Feature: Confirmations that name the specific record or field that will change
Pain point: Approve/deny gates a risky action but does not inform the decision
Label: Needs evidence
Differentiator angle: Field currently answers should-I-ask-permission but not what-to-show-when-asking; open space
Notes: Magentic-UI has the gating tiers; consequence-preview unresolved even for them
In plain terms: Before an agent changes real data, make the confirmation say exactly what will change (which record or field), not just a generic are-you-sure prompt. So people approve knowing the actual consequence.

Feature: Environment lifecycle legibility + checkpoint/branch a run
Pain point: Users cannot see what state an environment keeps across a run, when it stops existing, or cheaply branch/restore a run to try variants
Label: Needs evidence
Differentiator angle: DSec makes checkpoint/snapshot a backend feature; LayerLens's edge is making lifecycle legible and verifiable in the product (deterministic replay as a visible surface)
Notes: Single source and an infra paper not a UX study; needs a second source or confirmed user need to reach L1. Dedup: checked vs F-0001..F-0006, distinct (lifecycle/state legibility, not reliability readout or attribution)
In plain terms: Make it clear, while someone works in an environment, what information it remembers and when it will shut down, and let them save a checkpoint and branch off to try a variation. Frontier labs already do this in their backend plumbing; the opportunity is to make it visible and understandable in the product.

Feature: Establish ground truth for a user-built or prod-imported world (so realistic, free-form environments stay gradeable)
Pain point: A world a user hand-edits or mirrors from prod is realistic but arrives with no answer key, so agents cannot be graded against it deterministically and 'what is correct' is unknown
Label: Needs evidence
Differentiator angle: The crux of 'bring your real world and still get verifiable results'; extends answer-key-by-construction to worlds we did not mint (minted worlds use the deterministic grader, imported/edited worlds need ground truth established for actions/state/judge grading)
Notes: Internally derived (Javier + Claude, 2026-09-29), prompted by DSec's stateful/mutable model; not from external research, evidence is our own reasoning plus existing learned-world and actions/state/judge grader capabilities. Dedup: checked vs F-0001..F-0007, distinct (F-0007 = lifecycle/branch; this = ground truth for non-minted worlds). Needs a real user-need signal or external source to leave L0
In plain terms: Let users bring in their real (or freely built) world and still get trustworthy grading, by giving us a way to capture what 'correct' means for that world. Minted worlds come with the right answer built in; imported or edited ones do not, so this is about establishing that ground truth, so people can thoroughly test agents against their actual environment and still trust the verdict.
